explanations.answer: What is going to happen to Him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus takes the Twelve aside and begins to tell them what was going to happen to Him (Mark 10:32). He isn't handing out hotel info. He's telling them the hard part ahead of time, and I think that takes a steady heart.

explanations.answer: Where they will stay in the city
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think travel plans, since they're headed up the road to Jerusalem. But the text says Jesus began to tell them what was going to happen to Him (Mark 10:32). No room reservations in this one. It's much bigger than where anybody sleeps.

explanations.answer: How the temple will be rebuilt
explanations.explanation: Close, because Jerusalem is the destination, but the temple isn't the topic here. Mark 10:32 says Jesus began to tell the Twelve what was going to happen to Him. This talk is about Him, plain and personal.

Right, baker. Jesus says the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and "They will condemn Him to death…" (Mark 10:33). He says it straight, with no sugar on top. That's a heavy line, so I'll just say it plainly: this part is heavy.

Nope, the text says it outright. Jesus says the chief priests and scribes "…will condemn Him to death…" (Mark 10:33). He tells the Twelve exactly what is coming, and this is a heavy part of the passage.
Yes, three. Jesus says, "And after three days He will rise again." (Mark 10:34) The story doesn't end with the hard part. I'd say that's the line worth holding onto.

Seven is a good Bible number, I'll give you that. But Jesus says, "And after three days He will rise again." (Mark 10:34) Three is the number in this verse, and it comes right after the heaviest words.
Forty is a fair guess, but Jesus says, "And after three days He will rise again." (Mark 10:34) Three days, not forty. The count is short, and the promise is big.

True. James and John, the sons of Zebedee, come to Jesus and say, "Teacher, we want You to do for us whatever we ask." (Mark 10:35) They open with the blank check before they name the amount. Bold move, friends.

It's true, actually. Mark 10:35 has them say, "Teacher, we want You to do for us whatever we ask." That's how James and John, the sons of Zebedee, start. They ask for the promise first and the request second.

explanations.answer: Seats at His right and left
explanations.explanation: That's the one. They say, "Grant that one of us may sit at Your right hand and the other at Your left in Your glory." (Mark 10:37) Two brothers, two seats. I've asked for plenty of things in my day, but never the best chairs in the house.
Nice neighbors idea, but no houses come up. They ask that one of them may sit at Jesus' right hand and the other at His left in His glory (Mark 10:37). It's about seats, not real estate.

Their father, Zebedee, is named in Mark 10:35, but the text doesn't have them ask about him. What they ask is this: "Grant that one of us may sit at Your right hand and the other at Your left in Your glory." (Mark 10:37) It's all about those two seats.

Not quite, baker. Jesus says the opposite: "You do not know what you are asking…" (Mark 10:38). Then He asks them about the cup and the baptism. Honestly, I've ordered things in a hurry that I didn't understand either.
Right, it's false. Jesus replies, "You do not know what you are asking…" (Mark 10:38). Then He asks about the cup and the baptism. They had a request, but they didn't see the whole picture.
Yes, "We can," the brothers answer (Mark 10:39). That's their whole reply. Jesus then tells them, "You will drink the cup that I drink…" and they will be baptized with His baptism (Mark 10:39).
"Not yet" would've been a careful answer, but it's not what they said. The brothers answer, "We can," (Mark 10:39). Jesus then tells them, "You will drink the cup that I drink…" (Mark 10:39).
A humble answer, but the text has them say something shorter. The brothers answer, "We can," (Mark 10:39). Two words, and Jesus replies to them.

explanations.answer: They are not His to grant
explanations.explanation: That's right. Jesus says, "But to sit at My right or left is not Mine to grant. These seats belong to those for whom they have been prepared." (Mark 10:40) Granting them is not His to do. I'd say James and John got a plain answer.

explanations.answer: They belong to Moses and Elijah
explanations.explanation: Moses and Elijah are big names, but Jesus never names anyone for those seats. He says, "But to sit at My right or left is not Mine to grant. These seats belong to those for whom they have been prepared." (Mark 10:40) No names, just that they're prepared.

explanations.answer: They go to the oldest disciples
explanations.explanation: Age isn't mentioned in His answer. Jesus says, "But to sit at My right or left is not Mine to grant. These seats belong to those for whom they have been prepared." (Mark 10:40) Seniority doesn't come up, and He doesn't say who they're for.

Yes, you got it, baker. "When the ten heard about this, they became indignant with James and John." (Mark 10:41) Indignant means upset, and the text says it directly. That's the feeling the text gives for the ten.
I don't see any pats on the back here. Mark 10:41 says the ten "…became indignant with James and John." That means upset with them, not cheering them on.
No laughing in the text, baker. It says the ten "…became indignant with James and John." (Mark 10:41) Indignant is the opposite of amused. The text gives upset, not amusement.

Correct. Jesus says, "You know that those regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them." (Mark 10:42) The Gentiles are people who aren't Israelites. He starts with what they already see around them.

That's a kind guess, but it's not what Jesus says. He says the rulers of the Gentiles "…lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them." (Mark 10:42) Gentiles are non-Israelites, and the picture here is power over people.

Hands-off would be nice, but that's not the picture. Jesus says those regarded as rulers of the Gentiles "…lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them." (Mark 10:42) They're not leaving anybody alone. They're pressing authority on them.

Close, but Jesus says the opposite. After describing the Gentile rulers, He says, "But it shall not be this way among you." (Mark 10:43) He draws a clear line between how they do it and how His disciples should.
Yes, false. Jesus says, "But it shall not be this way among you." (Mark 10:43) He's pointing the Twelve toward a different way. Then He tells them what that way looks like.
That's the word. "Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant…" (Mark 10:43). Greatness shows up in serving, and Jesus says it plainly. Servant is the word He picks.

A master is exactly what the Gentile rulers act like, and Jesus says it shall not be that way among them. The verse reads, "Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant…" (Mark 10:43). Servant, not master.

Jesus is called Teacher by James and John in verse 35, so I see why it came to mind. But the word here is different: "Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant…" (Mark 10:43). Great means servant.

Yes, slave. Jesus says, "…and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all." (Mark 10:44) He goes even lower than servant, and that's the point. That's what He asks of whoever wants to be first.
Leader sounds right, but that's not the word in the verse. Jesus says, "…and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all." (Mark 10:44) For whoever wants to be first, the word is slave.
A judge sits up high, and Jesus is pointing the other way. The verse says, "…and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all." (Mark 10:44) Slave of all, not judge over all.
You got it, baker. Jesus says, "For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve…" (Mark 10:45). He says it about Himself. Serving is what He came to do.
Ruling is what the Gentile rulers do in verse 42, and that's not the picture here. Jesus says, "For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve…" (Mark 10:45). He came to serve.
Honor is a fair guess, but Jesus says, "For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve…" (Mark 10:45). Serving is the answer, and He means Himself. Being honored isn't what He names.
True. Jesus says the Son of Man came "…to give His life as a ransom for many." (Mark 10:45) That's the name He uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). I'd call it the biggest line in the passage.
It's true, baker. Jesus says the Son of Man came "…to give His life as a ransom for many." (Mark 10:45) The Son of Man is the name He uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). He ends the talk with His own life.
